## Overview

Slovaks are a West Slavic ethnic group and nation native to Slovakia. They share a common culture, ancestry, history, and speak the Slovak language. Slovakia has approximately 5.4 million autochthonous Slovaks, including about 4.7 million ethnic Slovaks within a total population of 5.4 million. Slovak minorities live in Austria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, and Ukraine, while Slovak immigrants and their descendants live in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Slovak folk culture developed through the history of Great Moravia, the Kingdom of Hungary, Habsburg rule, and Czechoslovakia. The sources describe Slovakia as having a very rich folk culture, including customs and social conventions shared with other nations of the former Habsburg monarchy.

## Music & performance

The sources identify Slovak as the language of the Slovaks and mention several Slovak composers: Eugen Suchoň, Ján Cikker, Mikuláš Moyzes, Alexander Moyzes, Vladimir Godar, and Peter Machajdík. They also state that Slovak culture developed within the historical contexts of Great Moravia, the Kingdom of Hungary, Habsburg rule, and Czechoslovakia. Great Moravia is associated with the mission of the Byzantine monks Cyril and Methodius, the development of the Glagolitic alphabet, and the use of Old Church Slavonic as an official and literary language.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources state that Slovakia exhibits folk customs and social conventions shared with other nations of the former Habsburg monarchy. The sources also provide no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for Slovakia concerning the Slovaks.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources mention Slovak historical writing and national revival activity. Georgius Papanek, also called Juraj Papánek, wrote *Historia gentis Slavae. De regno regibusque Slavorum...* in 1780, a history of the Slovak nation concerning the kingdom and kings of the Slovaks. His work became a basis for argumentation of the Slovak national revival movement. The sources also name Pavol Jozef Šafárik, Matej Bel, and Ján Kollár among Slovak polyhistors, and refer to a list of Slovak authors and poets.

## Language & religion

Slovak is a West Slavic language. The sources describe the early ancestors of Slovaks as having dialects divided between West Slavic varieties in western and eastern Slovakia and a non-West Slavic variety in central Slovakia; between the 8th and 9th centuries these dialects merged, laying the foundations of the later Slovak language. After the extinction of Proto-Slavic, Slovak evolved into an independent language between the 10th and 13th centuries. Anton Bernolák established a national standard based on the dialect of western Slovakia in 1787, while Ľudovít Štúr formed another standard based on the dialect of central Slovakia in 1843. Great Moravia used Old Church Slavonic as an official and literary language and was connected with Cyril and Methodius and the Glagolitic alphabet.
